body.text: Starting October 15, 2026, a merchant who receives a qualifying Unified Payments Interface (UPI) payment above Rs.2,000 will have to pay a merchant discount rate (MDR) of 0.4 per cent. A payment of Rs.3,000 will cost the merchant Rs.12. A payment of Rs.50,000 will cost Rs.200. The charge is capped at Rs.300 for transactions of Rs.75,000 and above. Small merchants classified under the person-to-person merchant framework, with UPI receipts of no more than Rs.1 lakh a month, remain exempt. Person-to-person money transfers will also remain free.

In introducing this measure, the Central government has sought to reassure consumers that UPI will remain free for them. It notes that merchants cannot add the MDR to a customer’s bill. According to the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) issued by the Department of Financial Services, consumers will continue to pay the posted price.

That last assurance is potentially problematic. The posted price of products depends on the merchant’s costs. A restaurant may be prevented from adding a separate UPI fee to the bill, but it can revise its prices. A retailer may not identify an MDR at checkout, but it can offer a smaller discount, change a promotion, or increase prices. A merchant can also encourage cash payments. It is hard to regulate the posted price.

Who is charged and who pays? The distinction is familiar in public finance. The statutory incidence of a tax/fee identifies the person legally responsible for it. The economic incidence of it is another matter. Where does the tax/fee ultimately land after businesses and consumers adjust their behaviour, as they are likely to?

An increase in fuel costs will first be paid by a transporter. Higher electricity rates will first appear on a factory’s bill. A rise in wholesale prices is initially borne by a retailer. Over time, businesses will try to recover at least part of these costs through prices, product sizes, service levels, or lower wages or payments to suppliers.

The same reasoning is likely to apply to UPI fee payment costs. MDR is deducted from the money that the merchant would have otherwise received. In other words, it is another element cost of goods sold, albeit a small one. The merchant’s ability to absorb it depends on its margins, competition and the share of sales on which it is charged.

The 0.4 per cent figure appears small, as it is expressed as a percentage of revenue. Merchants, however, do not keep all of their revenue. Consider a retailer earning a 4 per cent net margin on a transaction subject to the full fee. An MDR equal to 0.4 per cent of the sale would reduce that profit by 10 per cent, all else equal. For a business earning a 2 per cent margin, it would reduce profit by 20 per cent.

The calculation will vary across businesses. UPI may increase sales and some merchants may even save money when customers use UPI because of reduced cash handling costs and collection risks, and quick transaction settlement. These benefits help explain why merchants will continue to use UPI. However, it is not known whether all merchants can absorb a new fee without changing their posted prices.

The official claim that merchants have no economic incentive to raise their prices is rather strong. A merchant can value UPI, continue to accept it, and also attempt to recover part of its cost to protect its margins.
What some other evidence shows
Research shows that payment costs often reach consumers, even when merchants are formally charged.

A 2020 study of payment costs in the US and Canada, by Marie-Hélène Felt, Fumiko Hayashi, Joanna Stavins, and Angelika Welte, examined what happens when merchants incorporate card acceptance costs into the prices paid by all customers. Using a pass-through rate based on earlier empirical research, the authors found that cash and debit users effectively subsidised the higher cost of credit card transactions.

In a 2026 working paper, using a change in US debit card regulation, Mark Egan, Gregor Matvos, Amit Seru, Lulu Wang, and Vincent Yao found that interchange fees generate about $30 billion a year in transfers from cash and debit users to credit card users. Lower interchange fees led to lower prices and greater sales. Because credit card use rises with income, the authors estimate a transfer of $9.2 billion from households earning less than $1,50,000 to higher-income households.
The reverse mechanism, in which higher payment costs place upward pressure on prices, is the concern raised by the new MDR on UPI.

The MDR exemptions may not protect the small consumer or merchant. The argument is that the Rs.2,000 transaction threshold of MDR protects small consumers as more than 95 per cent of all merchant transactions are in this bracket. Further, small merchants with transactions of up to Rs.1 lakh a month through UPI are also exempt.

While these MDR protections are intended to protect small consumers and small merchants, they do not control who pays it. Consider a local kirana shop with UPI receipts exceeding Rs.1 lakh a month. If the merchant responds by adjusting prices across the shop, some of the cost may be spread across all customers, including those making purchases below Rs.2,000.

The proposed fee structure is also imbalanced. There is a 0.4 per cent rate for a transaction of Rs.3,000, but for payments that exceed Rs.75,000, there is a Rs.300 cap, lowering the per cent rate. Moreover, according to media reports, the Retailers Association of India considers the Rs.1 lakh monthly threshold for exemption of merchants from MDR to be too low and potentially excluding millions of microenterprises. So, some of these small merchants may encourage cash payments from customers to keep their UPI receipts below the threshold for MDR.

As most transactions still remain exempt from MDR, the net national effect on prices may perhaps be small. The concern is about equity in its effects. Prices for low-value products may rise, discounts may shrink, and some customers may be steered towards cash. Those changes can burden low-income consumers, whom the policy argues are fully protected by the proposed MDR.
Real costs, unclear answers

There is no question that payment providers need ongoing resources to maintain and improve a system of this scale. The government’s FAQ cites an industry estimate of roughly Rs.20,000 crore a year, but it does not publish the calculation behind that figure, the revenue expected from the MDR, or the proposed allocation of that revenue among banks, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), payment applications, and other intermediaries. (NPCI was set up by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Indian Banks’ Association (IBA) to create a robust payment and settlement infrastructure in the country.)

Who pays for the UPI system is not a new question. In a 2022 discussion paper on payment charges, the RBI raised the question of whether UPI should be subsidised, whether a charge should be a percentage of transaction value or a fixed amount, and whether the charge should be administered or market determined.
The RBI’s discussion paper also asked whether a fixed fee was more appropriate than a percentage charge. Those questions are just as relevant now.
UPI essentially transfers money between different bank accounts. Is the cost of processing a Rs.50,000 transfer likely to be more than 16 times the cost of processing a Rs.3,000 transfer?

The proposed MDR framework acknowledges this problem by applying a flat Rs.5 fee to paying for essential categories including fuel, utilities, school and college fees, insurance, and telecommunications.

The MDR imposition has been linked to India’s trade relationship with the US. US authorities have criticised the UPI policy as they say that it prevents foreign payment suppliers from competing on a level playing field in India.
The 2026 report of the US Trade Representative refers to the need for increased access for American payment companies in Indian markets within the UPI ecosystem.

On its part, India has denied the role of any foreign influence on the MDR decision. On August 8, 2026, a government release said: “Media reports have suggested that external influences may be driving policy changes. This is unfounded, completely false and misleading.”

Indeed, while US documents show no demand for an MDR, they do indicate a longstanding American concern that India’s payment policies favour domestic providers over international providers. That context warrants additional scrutiny as this may lay the ground for the entry of financial providers into the Indian market.

On measuring who might actually pay for the MDR, a first step would be to publish the rationale for the 0.4 per cent rate. What is the revenue that MDR is expected to bring in at this rate? What are the proposed plans for how to use the incremental revenue for maintaining and upgrading the UPI infrastructure? This will be useful for both policymakers and merchants and consumers to assess who is bearing the financial cost of the UPI system and whether the distribution of costs is equitable.

There should be a review of the effects of the MDR after a year of its implementation. The review should address the following questions: What are the price changes at affected and exempt merchants, reductions in price discounts, movement back to cash transactions, and transaction splitting? In particular, what are the differences across income groups, merchant sizes, and sectors?

If small merchants or low-income consumers end up bearing a disproportionate burden of the MDR costs, there should be a reconsideration of the Rs.1 lakh threshold and the standard 0.4 per cent rate. These thresholds should also be indexed to the consumer price index so that inflationary pressures do not push merchants into the chargeable category.

Importantly, public funding should be an integral part of the UPI model. The UPI model offers benefits beyond the value of a transaction, including financial inclusion and transaction visibility. The benefits accrue to government, banks, payment companies, merchants and consumers alike. Why then should small merchants or low-income consumers be asked to finance the system?

In sum, UPI as a public financial infrastructure is a significant policy achievement. A financing model is necessary for it to remain secure and reliable. However, a sustainable financing model needs to be fair and equitable.

The merchant will pay the MDR first. But it is also possible that the costs of the MDR may be passed on to consumers, including those whose payments never cross Rs.2,000. A credible MDR policy should measure and account for that possibility.
Raji Srinivasan is a professor of marketing at the University of Texas at Austin, US.
